q: What is the highest mountain in the British Isles?
fact: Ben Nevis stands 1,345 metres tall, near Fort William.

q: Which is the longest river in Ireland?
fact: The Shannon runs for about 360 kilometres.

q: Which is the largest island in the British Isles?
fact: Great Britain is the ninth largest island in the world.

q: What is the highest mountain in Wales?
fact: Snowdon is 1,085 metres high and has a railway to the top.

q: Which is the largest lake in the British Isles by surface area?
fact: Lough Neagh covers roughly 390 square kilometres in Northern Ireland.

q: Which is the largest loch in Great Britain by surface area?
fact: Loch Lomond is biggest by area, and Loch Ness is biggest by volume.

q: Which is the deepest lake in England?
fact: Wastwater in the Lake District is about 79 metres deep.

q: What is the highest mountain in England?
fact: Scafell Pike, in Cumbria, is 978 metres high.

q: Which river flows through Glasgow?
fact: The Clyde built Glasgow's wealth as a shipbuilding river.

q: Which river runs through the middle of York?
fact: The Ouse is joined in the city by the little River Foss.

q: Which river separates Liverpool from the Wirral?
fact: The Mersey is crossed by the famous ferry and two road tunnels.

q: Which London bridge has bascules that lift to let tall ships through?
fact: Tower Bridge opened in 1894 and still opens for tall vessels.

q: Which Irish province is Galway in?
fact: Galway is the biggest city in Connacht, on the west coast.

q: The name Dublin comes from the Irish for what?
fact: Dubh Linn means black pool, after a dark tidal pool on the Liffey.

q: Which river flows through Belfast?
fact: The Lagan runs past the Harland and Wolff yard into Belfast Lough.

q: Which strait separates Anglesey from mainland Wales?
fact: Telford's suspension bridge across the Menai Strait opened in 1826.

q: Which is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides?
fact: Skye is known as the Misty Isle.

q: Which is the longest river in the United Kingdom?
fact: The Severn is about 354 kilometres long, a little longer than the Thames.

q: In which year did Cardiff become the capital of Wales?
fact: Cardiff was named capital in 1955 and now has a Senedd by the bay.

q: In which county is the Giant's Causeway?
fact: The Causeway is a UNESCO World Heritage Site on the Antrim coast.

q: In which English county is Stonehenge?
fact: Stonehenge stands on Salisbury Plain.

q: Which Scottish city is nicknamed the Granite City?
fact: Much of Aberdeen is built from local grey granite that sparkles when wet.

q: How many countries make up the United Kingdom?
fact: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

q: Which is the largest county in Ireland by area?
fact: Cork is called the Rebel County, and it is a big one.

q: Which two cities did the world's first inter-city passenger railway join in 1830?
fact: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway used timetabled steam trains from day one.

q: On which island is the village with the very long name Llanfairpwll...gogogoch?
fact: The full name has 58 letters, and the station sign is a tourist favourite.

q: Which London park contains the Serpentine lake?
fact: The Serpentine was created in 1730 for Queen Caroline.

q: Which sea lies between Great Britain and Ireland?
fact: Ferries cross it from Holyhead, Liverpool and Cairnryan.

q: Which rail bridge, painted red, crosses the Firth of Forth?
fact: The Forth Bridge opened in 1890 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: In which county are the Cliffs of Moher?
fact: The cliffs rise up to 214 metres above the Atlantic.

q: Which is the largest lake in England?
fact: Windermere is about 18 kilometres long.

q: What is the highest peak in the Mourne Mountains, and in Northern Ireland?
fact: Slieve Donard is 850 metres high, and you can see the sea from the top.

q: Pen y Fan is the highest peak of which Welsh national park?
fact: Pen y Fan is 886 metres high.

q: Which of these cities is the furthest north?
fact: Aberdeen sits at about 57 degrees north.

q: In which year was the Battle of Hastings?
fact: William of Normandy beat King Harold and changed England for good.

q: What did the Romans call York?
fact: Mamucium is Manchester and Deva is Chester, but York was Eboracum.

q: In which year was the Great Fire of London?
fact: The fire began in a baker's shop in Pudding Lane.

q: In which year was the Battle of Bannockburn?
fact: Robert the Bruce's army beat a larger English force near Stirling.

q: Near which city was the Battle of Culloden fought in 1746?
fact: Culloden was the last pitched battle on British soil.

q: In which year was the Easter Rising?
fact: The Rising began in Dublin on Easter Monday, 24 April.

q: The Great Famine of the 1840s followed the failure of which crop?
fact: Blight ruined the potato harvests from 1845, and over a million people died.

q: Which Welsh leader began a great revolt against English rule in 1400?
fact: Glyndwr held a parliament at Machynlleth, and nobody knows how his story ended.

q: In which city did the Peterloo Massacre take place in 1819?
fact: A huge crowd gathered at St Peter's Field to demand the vote.

q: The Manchester Baby of 1948 was an early example of what?
fact: It ran its first program at the University of Manchester on 21 June 1948.

q: Which Liverpool club did the Beatles play at hundreds of times?
fact: The Cavern is on Mathew Street, and it is still going.

q: Which king signed Magna Carta in 1215?
fact: John sealed it at Runnymede, beside the Thames.

q: Which Roman emperor ordered a wall across northern Britain from AD 122?
fact: Hadrian's Wall is about 73 miles long, coast to coast.

q: What did the Vikings call York?
fact: Jorvik was an important Viking trading town.

q: In which Edinburgh palace did Mary, Queen of Scots, live?
fact: Holyrood stands at the foot of the Royal Mile.

q: In which year did Brian Boru win the Battle of Clontarf?
fact: Brian Boru beat the Vikings and their allies, though he died in the fighting.

q: Which castle was the setting for the 1969 investiture of the Prince of Wales?
fact: Edward I began Caernarfon Castle in 1283.

q: Which fortress in London holds the Crown Jewels?
fact: The Jewel House is guarded by Yeoman Warders.

q: Where was the Titanic built?
fact: Harland and Wolff built her, and she sailed from Southampton in 1912.

q: In which year was the Good Friday Agreement signed?
fact: It was signed in Belfast on 10 April 1998.

q: Who became the UK's first woman prime minister in 1979?
fact: Margaret Thatcher was born in Grantham, Lincolnshire.

q: In which year did the Acts of Union join England and Scotland?
fact: The two parliaments became one, based at Westminster.

q: Which book was made on William the Conqueror's orders in 1086?
fact: It recorded who owned what, and the tax collectors loved it.

q: Which Roman emperor was proclaimed at York in AD 306?
fact: The army declared Constantine emperor at Eboracum when his father died.

q: Who patented the flying shuttle in 1733, speeding up weaving?
fact: Kay's invention was a Lancashire first, and weavers were not all pleased.

q: Which illuminated manuscript is on show at Trinity College Dublin?
fact: The Book of Kells was made by monks around the year 800.

q: Which passage tomb in the Boyne Valley is older than Stonehenge and the pyramids?
fact: Newgrange is about 5,000 years old, and the winter solstice sun lights its chamber.

q: Who designed the new St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire?
fact: Wren's dome has dominated the London skyline since 1710.

q: In which year did the Welsh Senedd (then called the Assembly) first open?
fact: Devolution gave Wales its own elected body in Cardiff Bay.

q: Who is the patron saint of Scotland?
fact: His day is 30 November, and his saltire cross is on the flag.

q: Whose saint's day falls on 1 March?
fact: St David is the patron saint of Wales.

q: Which king was on the throne during the Great Fire of London?
fact: Charles II helped fight the flames himself, by some accounts.

q: Which Scottish loch is said to be home to a famous monster?
fact: Tales of a beast in the River Ness go back to the 6th century.

q: Which creature is on the flag of Wales?
fact: Y Ddraig Goch comes from a legend of red and white dragons.

q: In Irish folklore, whose wail warns of a death in the family?
fact: Banshee comes from bean si, meaning woman of the fairy mounds.

q: In Scottish and Irish tales, what are selkies?
fact: A selkie has to find its sealskin again to go home to the sea.

q: Which Yorkshire seaside town features in Bram Stoker's Dracula?
fact: Dracula arrives at Whitby in the shape of a huge black dog.

q: The Pendle witches were tried in 1612 in which county?
fact: They were tried at Lancaster, and Pendle Hill is a spooky walk to this day.

q: Which Somerset hill is linked to the legend of Avalon and King Arthur?
fact: St Michael's Tower still crowns the Tor.

q: In the Welsh legend of Beddgelert, what was Gelert?
fact: The village of Beddgelert is named for his grave.

q: In legend, why did Fionn mac Cumhaill build the Giant's Causeway?
fact: The giant wanted to fight Benandonner across the sea.

q: In Cornish folklore, what are the spirits of the tin mines called?
fact: Miners left a bit of pasty crust for the Knockers, for luck.

q: Which Scottish water horse lures people into lochs?
fact: Kelpies are shapeshifters, and they look like lovely horses until you climb on.

q: By tradition, how many ravens must be kept at the Tower of London?
fact: Legend says the kingdom falls if the ravens ever leave.

q: What are you said to gain by kissing the Blarney Stone?
fact: Blarney Castle is near Cork.

q: Who is said to have driven the snakes out of Ireland?
fact: Ireland never had snakes after the Ice Age, but it is a good story.

q: Which royal forest does Herne the Hunter haunt in Shakespeare's Merry Wives of Windsor?
fact: Herne's oak became a Windsor legend.

q: Burns Night on 25 January celebrates which poet?
fact: Haggis is addressed with a poem, then eaten.

q: What is the Green Man usually carved as?
fact: Green Men peer out of old churches all over England.

q: What does Y Ddraig Goch mean in English?
fact: It is the Welsh name for the dragon on the flag.

q: Bara brith is a traditional Welsh what?
fact: Bara brith means speckled bread, and it is nicest sliced with butter.

q: Haggis is traditionally served with neeps and what?
fact: Neeps are swede and tatties are potatoes.

q: Which Lancashire town gives its name to a currant-filled pastry?
fact: Eccles cakes are sometimes called squashed fly cakes.

q: Which hearty stew gave Liverpudlians their nickname?
fact: Scouse began as a sailors' stew, and the word stuck to the people.

q: A Yorkshire pudding is traditionally served with what?
fact: It was originally eaten first, with gravy, to fill people up.

q: Wallace's favourite cheese comes from which Yorkshire dale?
fact: Wensleydale cheese is made at Hawes, in the Dales.

q: In which Derbyshire town does the Bakewell tart come from?
fact: The tart is said to have started life by accident.

q: Kendal Mint Cake comes from which county?
fact: Kendal Mint Cake has been carried up mountains for generations.

q: What raises traditional Irish soda bread instead of yeast?
fact: The buttermilk reacts with the soda to make the bread rise.

q: Colcannon is mashed potato with what?
fact: Colcannon is traditionally eaten at Halloween.

q: Which type of bread is a key part of an Ulster fry?
fact: A farl is a triangular quarter of soda bread, fried till golden.

q: Cullen skink is a Scottish soup made from which smoked fish?
fact: Cullen is a village on the Moray coast.

q: Cranachan is made from raspberries, oats, cream and what?
fact: It was once a harvest dessert.

q: Which vegetable, called a turnip in Cornwall, goes in a Cornish pasty?
fact: A proper pasty has beef, potato, swede and onion, crimped to one side.

q: In a Cornish cream tea, what goes on the scone first?
fact: In Devon it is the other way round, and people have strong feelings.

q: Cawl is a traditional Welsh what?
fact: Cawl is traditionally made with lamb and leeks.

q: In which Dublin brewery is Guinness made?
fact: Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease there in 1759.

q: Barmbrack is a fruit loaf traditionally eaten at which festival?
fact: A ring baked in the loaf is said to mean marriage within the year.

q: Fat Rascals are a speciality of which famous York tearoom?
fact: A Fat Rascal is a fruity scone with a smiling face.

q: Which fizzy drink is nicknamed Scotland's other national drink?
fact: Irn-Bru is famously more popular in Scotland than the big American colas.

q: Boxty is a traditional Irish what?
fact: There is an old rhyme: boxty on the griddle, boxty on the pan.

q: In which city is the Sally Lunn bun famous?
fact: Sally Lunn's bun is served at one of the oldest houses in Bath.

q: Laverbread is made from what?
fact: Laverbread is boiled laver seaweed, often served with cockles and bacon.

q: Which is the only venomous snake native to Britain?
fact: Adders are shy and bite only if trodden on.

q: Which is the largest wild land animal in Britain?
fact: A big stag can weigh over 200 kilograms.

q: Wales is a stronghold of which once-rare bird of prey with a forked tail?
fact: Red kites were down to a handful of pairs in mid Wales at their lowest.

q: Which seabird nests in burrows and has a colourful bill in summer?
fact: Puffins are also called sea parrots.

q: Which bird is the fastest animal on Earth, diving at over 300 km/h?
fact: Peregrines have moved into cities, and nest on cathedrals.

q: Which County Clare landscape mixes Arctic and Mediterranean flowers?
fact: The Burren's limestone pavement is full of wildflowers in spring.

q: What is a group of rooks called?
fact: Rooks nest together in noisy rookeries.

q: Where do Britain's grey squirrels originally come from?
fact: They were released in the late 1800s, and they have spread widely.

q: What is a baby hare called?
fact: Leverets are born furred and with their eyes open.

q: Which animal lives in a sett?
fact: Setts can be centuries old, with many tunnels.

q: What is an otter's home called?
fact: A drey is a squirrel's nest, and a sett is a badger's.

q: Which plant is the national emblem of Scotland?
fact: Legend says a thistle once saved the Scots from a night attack.

q: Which rock are the White Cliffs of Dover made of?
fact: The chalk is made of tiny sea creatures from about 90 million years ago.

q: What is a haar on the east coast of Scotland?
fact: A haar rolls in off the North Sea, often in spring and early summer.

q: Which animal has pups born with a white coat that they moult after a few weeks?
fact: Britain and Ireland host a large share of the world's grey seals.

q: Which small mammal has a hibernation nest called a hibernaculum?
fact: Hedgehogs can sleep through months of cold weather in a leaf pile.

q: What are Nessie's two types in the Fieldbook?
fact: Nessie is found at Loch Ness, naturally.

q: Which creature is the first form of the red squirrel line?
fact: Kindlet evolves into Emberdrey at level 16.

q: At what level does Spikkin evolve into Bramblehog?
fact: Bramblehog later becomes Thornsow at level 32.

q: What does Basaltling evolve into at level 28?
fact: Basaltling is found around the Giant's Causeway.

q: Where does the Fieldbook say Bran's Raven is found?
fact: Bran is a legendary creature, linked to the ravens of the Tower.

q: What type is Kindlet?
fact: Hearth is strong against Hedgerow, Frost and Iron.

q: At what level does Rillotter evolve into Spatelord?
fact: Holtling becomes Rillotter at 16, and Spatelord is Brook and Night.

q: Which item evolves Jetling into Jetwhitby?
fact: Whitby jet is fossilised wood from the Jurassic.

q: Croakle evolves into Bufomire at level 22 in what weather?
fact: Toads love a wet evening.

q: At what time of day does Pepperling evolve into Sootwing?
fact: Peppered moths turned dark in sooty Manchester in the 1800s.

q: How many creature types are there in the Fieldbook?
fact: From Kin and Hedgerow to Night, there are sixteen.

q: Brook moves are super effective against which type?
fact: Water on fire, which makes sense. Stone is also on the list.

q: Hearth moves are super effective against which type?
fact: Hearth is also super effective against Hedgerow and Iron.

q: Kin-type moves have no effect on which type?
fact: It is hard to hit a ghost with a hug.

q: Which Fieldbook creature is based on Britain's only free-ranging reindeer?
fact: Calfrein evolves into Reindeer at level 30, in the Cairngorms.

q: At what level does Caperling evolve into Capercaillie?
fact: Capercaillie are the world's largest grouse.

q: Which Sheffield creature evolves into Steelheart at level 34?
fact: Stainless steel was invented in Sheffield in 1913.

q: Which Belfast creature evolves into Samsonian at level 32?
fact: Samsonian is named for the Harland and Wolff cranes.

q: Which Fieldbook creature is found around Edinburgh and the Forth Bridge?
fact: Railspark is Iron and Storm.

q: At what level does Chipgull evolve into Pierlord?
fact: Herring gulls love chips and rooftops.

q: Which Fieldbook creature is based on London's ring-necked parakeets?
fact: Parakit becomes Squawkster at level 26.

q: What are the types of Y Ddraig Goch, the Welsh dragon?
fact: The red dragon is found at Dinas Emrys.

q: Where in the Fieldbook is Legionette, the Roman soldier, found?
fact: Legionette evolves into Centurion at level 30.

q: Which Fieldbook creature is the edible dormouse?
fact: Glisglis can be found in Sherwood.

q: Which island does the Fieldbook place Loaghtan, the mouse-coloured sheep, on?
fact: Loaghtan is Manx for mouse-coloured.

q: At what level does Barnling evolve into Hushwing?
fact: Barn owls find prey in the dark by hearing alone.

q: What are Enbarr's types, Manannan's sea-galloping horse?
fact: In Irish myth, Enbarr can gallop over the waves.

q: What are the types of the Highland fairy dog Cu-Sith?
fact: Three barks from the Cu-Sith are said to foretell a death.

q: What are the types of the Lambton Worm?
fact: The legend says the Lambton family was cursed for nine generations.

q: Which famous shop began as a penny bazaar stall in Leeds's Kirkgate Market in 1884?
fact: Michael Marks's sign read: Don't ask the price, it's a penny.

q: Standedge Tunnel, the longest, highest and deepest canal tunnel in Britain, carries which canal under the Pennines?
fact: It runs over three miles from Diggle to Marsden and opened in 1811.

q: On which day do brass bands tour the Saddleworth villages playing contest marches?
fact: Bands dash between villages by coach and play to a judge who can't see them.

q: Under what surname did the Brontë sisters first publish their novels?
fact: Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell were Charlotte, Emily and Anne.

q: Which Brontë sister wrote Wuthering Heights?
fact: It was published in 1847, a year before Emily died.

q: What guards the steps of Leeds Town Hall, said to come alive when the clock strikes midnight?
fact: The lions were added in 1867, nine years after Queen Victoria opened the hall.

q: Where is England's only wild population of mountain hares?
fact: They were brought over from Scotland in the 1800s and turn white in winter.

q: Forced rhubarb from the Rhubarb Triangle is picked by what light?
fact: Light stops the stalks growing, so the forcing sheds stay dark.

q: Which Leeds mill was built to look like an Egyptian temple, with sheep grazing on its roof?
fact: It was a flax mill built for John Marshall in the 1830s.

q: In which town did northern clubs meet in 1895 to found what became rugby league?
fact: They met at the George Hotel, in a row over paying players for time lost from work.

q: Which six towns make up Stoke-on-Trent?
a: Tunstall, Burslem, Hanley, Stoke, Fenton and Longton
wrong: Leek, Burslem, Hanley, Stoke, Stone and Longton
Tunstall, Crewe, Hanley, Stoke, Fenton and Leek
Burslem, Hanley, Stafford, Stoke, Uttoxeter and Longton
fact: Arnold Bennett called them the Five Towns, and left out Fenton.

q: What was a saggar, in a Potteries bottle oven?
a: A fireclay box that held pots during firing
fact: The saggar maker's bottom knocker made the bases. It was a real job.

q: Which Spitfire designer grew up in the Potteries?
fact: The Spitfire first flew in 1936, the year before Mitchell died.

q: What is a Staffordshire oatcake?
fact: They are rolled round cheese, bacon or sausage and eaten warm.

q: In which year was the Staffordshire Hoard found?
fact: It holds over 3,500 pieces, mostly gold and garnet war gear.

q: Which animal lived wild on the Roaches for decades after escaping from a private zoo?
fact: They were let out around the start of the Second World War.

q: Which author was named after a lake near Leek?
fact: His parents met at Rudyard Lake in 1863.

q: Which medieval poem's Green Chapel is often linked to Lud's Church?
a: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
fact: The poem is written in a dialect from the north-west Midlands.

q: What does Saggit evolve into?
fact: Bottle ovens once crowded the Potteries skyline, about 2,000 of them.

q: In which year did Blackpool Tower open?
fact: It was inspired by the Eiffel Tower and stands 158 metres high.

q: Which British seaside town is the only one with three piers?
fact: North Pier, Central Pier and South Pier opened in 1863, 1868 and 1893.

q: What did people call the eight arc lamps that lit Blackpool's promenade in 1879?
fact: The Illuminations as we know them began in 1912 and now run for about six miles.

q: Blackpool's tramway, still running today, opened in which year?
fact: It is one of the first electric street tramways in the world, and the oldest still running.

q: Where on the Sefton coast do a hundred cast-iron men stand gazing out to sea?
fact: The artwork, Another Place, arrived in 2005 and was made permanent in 2007.

q: Which rare mammal lives in the pinewoods at Formby?
fact: Squirrelpox killed most of Formby's reds in 2008, but the population has recovered.

q: Which swans fly in from Iceland to winter at Martin Mere?
fact: Whoopers have a yellow wedge on the bill; mute swans have orange.

q: Which Lancashire dish is lamb and onion, topped with sliced potatoes and baked slowly?
fact: It was a mill-town favourite: put in the oven in the morning, ready by teatime.

q: Which footballer starred in the 1953 'Matthews Final' for Blackpool?
fact: Blackpool came back from 3-1 down to beat Bolton 4-3.

q: Southport Pier is the second-longest pier in Britain. Which is the longest?
fact: Southport Pier opened in 1860, and at low tide its end often stands over sand.

q: Who designed the Clifton Suspension Bridge?
fact: Brunel won the competition aged 24; the bridge was finished in 1864, after his death.

q: What was the SS Great Britain the first big ship to combine?
a: An iron hull and a screw propeller
wrong: A steel hull and paddle wheels
fact: She was launched in Bristol in 1843 and came home to the same dock in 1970.

q: In 1497 John Cabot sailed from Bristol to North America in which ship?
fact: A replica of the Matthew is moored in Bristol's Floating Harbour.

q: Which event fills the sky over Ashton Court, Bristol, every August?
fact: The Bristol International Balloon Fiesta began in 1979.

q: Which supersonic airliner was built at Filton, near Bristol?
fact: The last Concorde ever to fly landed at Filton in November 2003.

q: Which bird of prey nests on the cliffs of the Avon Gorge?
fact: In a dive a peregrine can pass 300 kilometres an hour.

q: In 1963 people in Bristol boycotted what, to end a colour bar?
fact: The Bristol Bus Boycott won on 28 August 1963.

q: Which film star was born Archibald Leach in Bristol?
fact: His statue stands in Millennium Square.

q: Which Swansea line became the world's first passenger railway service, in 1807?
fact: The Oystermouth Railway began carrying fare-paying passengers in a horse-drawn carriage in March 1807, and closed in 1960.

q: In 1956 Gower became Britain's first what?
fact: Gower, Gŵyr in Welsh, was the first AONB in Britain.

q: The 'Red Lady of Paviland', found on Gower in 1823, turned out to be what?
a: A young man about 33,000 years old
fact: The bones were stained with red ochre; it is the oldest known ceremonial burial in western Europe.

q: Which poet called Swansea an 'ugly, lovely town'?
fact: Dylan Thomas was born at 5 Cwmdonkin Drive, Swansea, in 1914.

q: What does the Welsh name for Swansea, Abertawe, mean?
fact: The English name is probably Norse: Sveinn's island or inlet.

q: What is laverbread made from?
fact: Laver seaweed is boiled for hours into a black purée; Richard Burton called it Welshman's caviar.

q: Which metal earned 19th-century Swansea the nickname 'Copperopolis'?
fact: Ore was shipped in from Cornwall, Chile and Cuba to be smelted with Welsh coal.

q: In the Welsh midwinter custom of the Mari Lwyd, what is carried door to door?
a: A horse's skull on a pole
fact: The party challenges each house to the pwnco, a contest of rhymes, before being let in.

q: Which Devon cathedral has the longest unbroken stretch of medieval Gothic vaulting in the world?
fact: Exeter Cathedral's vault runs for about 96 metres without a break.

q: From which port did the Mayflower finally sail for America in 1620?
fact: The Mayflower left Southampton with the Speedwell, but the leaky Speedwell was left behind at Plymouth.

q: On a Devon cream tea, what goes on the scone first?
fact: In Cornwall it's jam first, and the argument has been going on for generations.

q: What game was Sir Francis Drake said to be playing when the Armada was sighted?
fact: The story places the game on Plymouth Hoe in 1588.

q: What is the nickname of Plymouth Argyle?
fact: The Grecians are Exeter City; the Pilgrims are named after the Mayflower's passengers.

q: Where on Dartmoor did letterboxing begin in 1854?
fact: A guide, James Perrott, left a bottle there for walkers' calling cards.

q: Which black-and-white wader, the RSPB's emblem, winters in big flocks on the Exe Estuary?
fact: Avocets returned to breed in England in the 1940s after a century away.

q: Smeaton's Tower on Plymouth Hoe first stood as a lighthouse on which rocks?
fact: It was taken down and rebuilt on the Hoe in the 1880s when the rock beneath it wore away.

q: Which Dartmoor road is haunted by the Hairy Hands?
fact: The stories centre on the stretch near Postbridge.

q: Enniskillen stands on an island between which two lakes?
fact: Its Irish name, Inis Ceithleann, means Ceithleann's island.

q: In legend, the sod Finn McCool scooped out to make Lough Neagh became which island?
fact: The giant was aiming at a Scottish rival and missed.

q: Boxty, a Fermanagh favourite, is a pancake made mainly from what?
fact: It mixes grated raw potato with mashed potato, cooked on a griddle.

q: Which two famous writers both went to Portora Royal School in Enniskillen?
wrong: James Joyce and W. B. Yeats
C. S. Lewis and Seamus Heaney
fact: Beckett won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1969.

q: Where do the eels of Lough Neagh hatch?
fact: They cross the Atlantic as tiny see-through glass eels.

q: On which Fermanagh island does a 12th-century round tower stand by St Molaise's monastery?
fact: The tower is about 30 metres tall, one of the finest in Ireland.

q: What does Neagheen, the Lough Neagh eel, evolve into?
fact: Mór is Irish for big, and -een means small.

q: Which county is known as the Orchard County?
fact: Armagh Bramley apples have had protected status since 2012.

q: What is the highest mountain in County Donegal?
fact: Errigal is 751 metres high and made of quartzite, which glows pink at sunset.

q: Which famous history of Ireland was compiled by four scholars in the 1630s?
a: The Annals of the Four Masters
fact: Led by the friar Mícheál Ó Cléirigh, they recorded Irish history year by year up to 1616.

q: What does the Irish name Dún na nGall mean?
fact: The foreigners were probably Vikings with a fort on the River Eske.

q: Which one-eyed king of the Fomorians was said to live on Tory Island?
fact: In the legend, Balor was killed by his grandson Lugh with a sling-stone through the eye.

q: Which bird of prey was reintroduced to Glenveagh National Park from 2000?
fact: The chicks came from Scotland, after golden eagles had been gone from Ireland for most of a century.

q: What is the most northerly point of the island of Ireland?
fact: Malin Head is in Inishowen, County Donegal, and gives its name to a Shipping Forecast sea area.

q: Tory Island is unusual for choosing its own what?
fact: The King of Tory has no crown or palace; he welcomes visitors and speaks up for the island.

q: Which Donegal town is Ireland's biggest fishing port?
fact: Killybegs trawlers land mackerel, herring and blue whiting.

q: In which year was the Treaty of Limerick signed?
fact: It ended the Williamite War in Ireland; tradition says it was signed on the Treaty Stone.

q: Irish coffee was first made in 1943 at which flying-boat port?
fact: Chef Joe Sheridan made it for cold passengers off a flying boat that had turned back.

q: Munster beat the New Zealand All Blacks 12-0 in 1978 at which ground?
fact: It was the first time an Irish side had beaten the All Blacks.

q: Shannon Airport opened the world's first what, in 1947?
fact: The idea was Brendan O'Regan's.

q: When it opened in 1929, Ardnacrusha on the Shannon was the world's largest what?
fact: It was built by Siemens as the Shannon Scheme.

q: Which Pulitzer-winning memoir describes a poor childhood in Limerick?
fact: Frank McCourt published it in 1996.

q: Which famous scientist was born in Shrewsbury in 1809?
fact: Darwin was born at The Mount in Shrewsbury and went to school in the town.

q: In which year did Abraham Darby I first smelt iron with coke at Coalbrookdale?
fact: Coke smelting made cheap iron possible and helped start the Industrial Revolution.

q: What was the Iron Bridge in Shropshire the first major bridge in the world to be made of?
fact: It was cast at Coalbrookdale by Abraham Darby III and opened in 1781.

q: Which Shropshire town's Olympian Games, first held in 1850, helped inspire the modern Olympics?
fact: Pierre de Coubertin visited the Wenlock Olympian Games in 1890.

q: According to legend, who sits in the Devil's Chair on the Stiperstones when the mist comes down?
fact: Legend says that if the Stiperstones ever sink into the ground, England will fall.

q: To go 'all round the Wrekin' means what?
a: To take the long way round
fact: The Wrekin is a lone hill east of Shrewsbury, and the old Shropshire toast is 'to all friends round the Wrekin'.

q: What is a Shrewsbury cake?
fact: Shrewsbury cakes have been baked in the town since at least the 1500s.

q: Ditherington Flax Mill in Shrewsbury, built in 1797, was the first building in the world with what?
fact: Its cast-iron frame makes it the grandfather of the skyscraper.

q: Which pub did Crick and Watson walk into in 1953 to announce they'd found the structure of DNA?
fact: Crick told the lunchtime crowd they had found the secret of life.

q: What does the name Ely mean?
fact: Monks in Ely once took rents paid in eels, counted in sticks of twenty-five.

q: Who held the Isle of Ely against William the Conqueror in 1070 and 1071?
fact: When the Isle fell, Hereward escaped into the fens and vanished from history.

q: How were the Norfolk Broads formed?
fact: The botanist Joyce Lambert proved it in the 1950s.

q: Why are Norwich City nicknamed the Canaries?
a: Flemish weavers bred canaries in Norwich
wrong: Their first ground was a bird shop
They once played in a mine
A canary landed on the pitch in 1902
fact: The Strangers, Protestant weavers from the Low Countries, settled in Norwich from 1565.

q: What sits on top of the Corpus Clock in Cambridge?
fact: Chronophage means time-eater. Stephen Hawking unveiled the clock in 2008.

q: Who supposedly built Cambridge's Mathematical Bridge without bolts, according to the myth?
fact: Newton died in 1727; the bridge was built by James Essex in 1749.

q: Which was the National Trust's first nature reserve, from 1899?
fact: Victorian naturalists wanted to save the fen's insects.

q: Which anchoress wrote the earliest surviving book in English known to be by a woman?
fact: Her Revelations of Divine Love says: all shall be well.

q: In which year was Thomas Becket murdered in Canterbury Cathedral?
fact: Four knights killed him on 29 December 1170; he was made a saint in 1173.

q: Which operation, planned in the tunnels under Dover Castle, rescued soldiers from Dunkirk in 1940?
fact: About 338,000 soldiers were brought home between 26 May and 4 June 1940.

q: Which Brighton seafront line, opened in 1883, is the oldest operating electric railway in the world?
fact: Magnus Volk built it along the beach; it still runs in summer.

q: For whom was Brighton's Royal Pavilion built?
a: The Prince Regent, later George IV
fact: John Nash gave it its Indian domes and minarets between 1815 and 1823.

q: What are the White Cliffs of Dover made of?
fact: The chalk is built from the tiny limy plates of ancient sea algae.

q: What is an oast house used for?
fact: The white cowl on top turns with the wind to draw warm air through the hops.

q: What kind of creature was the knucker of Lyminster in Sussex?
wrong: A sea serpent of the Thames
fact: Legend says it was killed with a poisoned pie; the Slayer's Slab in Lyminster church is said to mark the hero's grave.

q: Who wrote The Canterbury Tales?
fact: Chaucer's pilgrims ride from the Tabard Inn in Southwark to Becket's shrine.

q: What colour are the telephone boxes in Hull?
fact: Hull's council ran its own telephone service from 1902, and its boxes have no crown.

q: In which year did the Humber Bridge open?
fact: It was the world's longest single-span suspension bridge for sixteen years.

q: Which Hull-born MP led the campaign in Parliament against the slave trade?
fact: Wilberforce was born on Hull's High Street in 1759; his house is now a museum.

q: Lincoln Cathedral was the tallest building in the world until its spire fell in which year?
fact: It held the record for over two hundred years, taller than the Great Pyramid.

q: Which famous 1215 document has an original copy in Lincoln Castle?
fact: Only four original copies of the 1215 charter survive.

q: The first tanks were built in which city?
fact: William Foster and Co. built Little Willie in Lincoln in 1915.

q: Where is Britain's tallest standing stone?
fact: The Rudston Monolith, about 7.6 metres tall, stands beside All Saints Church.

q: What is a Hull patty?
fact: Put it in a bread cake and it's a pattie butty.

q: Which poet was librarian at the University of Hull for thirty years?
fact: His statue at Hull Paragon hurries for a train.

q: In which year was Hull UK City of Culture?
fact: A 75-metre wind turbine blade called Blade lay across Queen Victoria Square.

q: When did the Forth Bridge, the great red railway bridge near Edinburgh, open?
fact: It opened on 4 March 1890 and in 2015 it was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: Which is the oldest university in Scotland?
fact: The University of St Andrews was founded in 1413, the third oldest in the English-speaking world.

q: Which ship, built in Dundee, carried Captain Scott to the Antarctic in 1901?
fact: Discovery was built by the Dundee Shipbuilders Company and is back home in Dundee as a museum ship.

q: In which year did the first Tay Bridge fall in a storm with a train on it?
fact: It fell on the night of 28 December 1879. Nobody on the train survived.

q: Who wrote 'The Tay Bridge Disaster', often called the worst poem in the English language?
fact: McGonagall lived in Dundee and was proud of his poems. Audiences threw things at him. He kept going.

q: Dundee was famous for three things: jute, jam and what?
fact: Jute mills, Keiller's marmalade and DC Thomson's newspapers and comics, still published in Dundee.

q: What goes on top of a proper Dundee cake?
fact: Rings of blanched almonds, pressed in before baking.

q: Which old stone bridge crosses the Swilcan Burn on the Old Course at St Andrews?
fact: Golfers stop on it for a photograph on the way up the 18th.

q: Runners on the West Sands at St Andrews open which 1981 film?
fact: The film is about the runners Eric Liddell and Harold Abrahams at the 1924 Olympics.

q: Which Fife village, kept as it was in the 1600s, had the sole right to make iron girdles for baking?
fact: King James VI granted the Culross hammermen the girdle monopoly in 1599.

q: Richard Trevithick's Penydarren locomotive of 1804 hauled what along the Merthyr tramroad?
a: Ten tons of iron and about seventy men
fact: It was the first journey by a steam locomotive on rails, and it won a bet of 500 guineas.

q: Which Merthyr man was hanged in Cardiff in 1831 after the Rising?
fact: Many believed Richard Lewis, known as Dic Penderyn, was innocent. His last words are said to have been 'O Arglwydd, dyma gamwedd'.

q: Which Scot, who first went down a mine aged ten, was elected MP for Merthyr Tydfil in 1900?
fact: Hardie became the first leader of the Labour Party and held the Merthyr seat until his death in 1915.

q: Which Welsh dish is a broth of lamb, leeks and root vegetables?
fact: Cawl is often called the national dish of Wales, and traditionally tastes better the next day.

q: What does the Welsh word 'cwm' mean?
fact: The south Wales coalfield is a comb of cwms, and the Rhondda is two of them: Fawr and Fach.

q: In which year did the Blaenavon Industrial Landscape become a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
fact: It was the first industrial site in Wales to be listed.

q: Roughly how far down does the cage take visitors at Big Pit?
fact: Big Pit closed as a colliery in 1980 and reopened as the National Coal Museum, with ex-miners as guides.

q: What did Sidney Gilchrist Thomas and Percy Gilchrist test at Blaenavon in 1878?
a: A way to make steel from iron rich in phosphorus
fact: Their 'basic' process opened up the world's phosphoric iron ores to steelmaking.

q: A medical aid society in which Welsh mining town inspired the National Health Service?
fact: Tredegar's miners paid a few pence a week for medical care. Aneurin Bevan, born there, launched the NHS in 1948.

q: Which Merthyr-born composer wrote the love song 'Myfanwy'?
fact: Parry was born in Merthyr in 1841, worked in the ironworks as a boy and wrote 'Myfanwy' in 1875.

q: What are Welsh cakes traditionally cooked on?
wrong: A baking tray in the oven
A hot stone in a river
fact: Picau ar y maen are 'cakes on the stone': flour, butter, currants, sugar and a pinch of spice.

q: Who built Cyfarthfa Castle above his Merthyr ironworks in 1824?
fact: The castle looked down on the furnaces, and is now a museum and art gallery.
